paragraphs: After Yao Chang moved into the separate residence in the capital, another snowfall came to Chang’an.

When Fu Jian left the palace, the old ceremonial canopy beyond the east gate had already been half dismantled. Months earlier, when the Qin army returned north, the ritual officials had proposed a triumphal welcome, and red silk had been tied to the canopy supports. Fu Jian had ordered the drums and musicians dismissed. Now a carpenter on the beams was pulling out the last bamboo wedges. A faded strip of red silk drifted down in the wind and settled softly on the imperial road.
Fu Jian bent to pick it up and handed it to an attendant.
“Send whatever timber can still be used to repair the military granaries.”

He did not return to the palace. Ordering a few attendants to change horses and follow him, he rode straight out of the north gate. Fu Rong caught up with the party outside the city. When he saw the imperial horse turn southwest, he knew where his brother was going. He reined in and did not follow.

The pines beside the path to Wang Meng’s tomb had grown tall. A few young cypresses newly planted before the stele had not yet risen above the stone railing; fine sand dusted their needles. The old caretaker was chopping wood when he saw the imperial horse. In a panic he hid his axe among the logs. Fu Jian told him to go on chopping, then sent his attendants beyond the trees.
He stood before the stele for a long time before realizing he had brought no wine.
“Jinglüe, I have come empty-handed again.”
A small bird fluttered in the treetops. Farther off, the chop of the old man’s axe continued fitfully. No one stopped for the emperor’s murmur.

From his robe Fu Jian drew a military map stained by rain. Vermilion ink marked the camps on the northern bank of the Fei, and circles enclosed three crossings. Beneath it lay half a sheet of withdrawal orders, approved in his own hand, the ink already faded. There was also a register of the sick, wounded, and missing civilian porters that the Department of State Affairs was checking anew. Its corners had gone soft from handling.
“You urged me to wait ten years. They have not even passed, and already I have reached the Fei River.”

He sat on the stone steps below the stele. At court, men spoke loudly of uniting the realm. Only here could he admit that the river was not very wide, that cavalry could cross if they found a ford, and that among his hundred and fifty thousand soldiers, those eager to cross were certainly no fewer than those who favored returning north.

That day he had imagined Xie Xuan’s vanguard reaching midstream and Qin horsemen sweeping down from the heights, battle flags unfurling suddenly through the river mist. He had seen too many victories like it. Precisely because he had seen them, he knew that once the war drums sounded, no one could foresee the road home for the last soldier in the ranks.

“For years I thought of it. I even gave the scholars of the south their faces in my mind: coming to Chang’an with their families, as the former Yan ministers once did, bowing before me and saying that all under heaven had finally been united.”
He smiled at himself.
“But what I saw beside the Fei was a grain cart.”

It had sunk into a rain-soaked slope. More than ten civilian porters pushed at it without budging it while the escorting clerk shouted himself hoarse. Farther away the distant horns and drums of the Jin army sounded faintly; the cart driver cared only whether the mule in the traces would stand again. Fu Jian had not gone to help. He was the Heavenly King commanding all the armies, and to learn even which province the cart belonged to he would have had to order someone to search the registers.
“Jinglüe, if you had been there, perhaps you would have scolded me.” He rubbed his brow. “I did not take my army across, yet I have already carried away more than half the realm’s grain and money.”

He had nothing to add. He thought of the night Wang Meng lay dying: the rain sounding just so, as the old minister compelled him to set each promise down in an imperial decree. Wang Meng’s hand had been cold as unlit charcoal, yet he had persisted in asking about the crown prince, the surrendered generals, and the control of the army. Back then Fu Jian had wished the ten years could shrink into a single night. So long as a man was alive, he had thought, the days could be bent to his will.
Now fresh moss greened the stele, and that hand on the sickbed would never move again. Only now did he see that ten years were no more than the time it took for the world to turn once.
“I still want to unite the realm,” he said softly. “That, I fear, will not change before I die.”
Outside the grove came the faint sound of horses chewing their fodder. Fu Jian folded away the map but left the register of the wounded and sick upon his knees.

“Back in Chang’an today, some call me a coward for refusing battle. Some resent the unpaid rewards. Others say the crown prince and Fu Rong stood between me and greatness. I do not fear their curses. I fear that next year someone will bring another map and promise that this time victory is certain. I shall feel the old hunger, and forget the people named in these papers.”

He rose before the stele, brushed fallen pine needles from his sleeves, and gave the smallest of bows. There was no decree, no drum music. After he had gone, the caretaker noticed a patch of wet earth below the monument, marked by a shallow, winding line someone had drawn with a fingertip. He brought water to wash the steps, uncertain whether to preserve the mark or wipe it away. In the end, he washed only the ground beside it.

For more than ten days afterward, Fu Jian did not again convene the grand debate that had divided his empire into two discordant voices. Instead he summoned in separate groups the officials responsible for frontier affairs, the Central Army Office, and the Court for State Guests. On his desk lay dispatches from the Fei, maps of the border passes of the two states, grain prices from the markets of Longxi, and letters from families that had made their way from Xiangyang.
The first matter was the prisoners.

The officer responsible for checking identities offered a list of surrendered soldiers from Xiangyang. Some had married and had children; some wished to return south of the Yangtze; others had long since been taken away by powerful local families to work their fields. An official asked whether all should be handed over if Jin envoys demanded their return.
“Let them speak for themselves first,” Fu Jian said.
“Who is to ask them?”

“The people who keep their registers now. And when relatives come to claim them, do not judge by surnames alone. Some children were only seven when they left home. Grown to adulthood, they may have forgotten even their old names.”

He ordered each frontier exchange point to prepare testimony identifying relatives and proof of the home districts. No one was to be transferred in haste on the strength of a single total from a military register. Zhu Xu was still living as a minister of Jin at the Court for State Guests. He had been invited to the hall that day because Fu Jian wanted to know how the people once living in Xiangyang would regard such a return.
After listening, Zhu Xu asked only, “Those who do not wish to return may still remember their homeland.”
“What else would hold them here?”
“If they go back, their land may have passed to another owner, and their families may no longer be there.”

Fu Jian ordered the remark recorded in the proceedings. Zhu Xu watched the moving brush. Only after a long silence did he ask, “If someone should ask for my return to Jin, would Your Majesty permit it?”

Fu Jian did not answer at once. He still hated to let a stubbornly faithful enemy minister return south, a man whose loyalty could make the emperor himself uncomfortable. Yet he also knew that treating Zhu Xu with honor in Chang’an could not undo what had happened beneath the walls of Xiangyang.
“When the two sides have agreed on an exchange, your name will be entered as well.”

Zhu Xu bowed but did not offer thanks. On the way back to his lodging he carried a letter from an old friend, the envelope still marked with mud from a Jiang–Huai ferry. He did not know whether the sender still lived. He carefully folded the paper and slipped it back into his sleeve.
The second matter was trade across the frontier.

The routes north of the Huai had been broken for years. Salt merchants took roundabout roads, cloth merchants traveled at risk, and smuggling across the border had never ceased. Officials of the Court for State Guests presented terrain maps of three possible regulated markets, with the customary heavy taxes already written into the proposal. Fu Jian lifted the sheet and handed it to Fu Rong. “Let the merchant caravans get through first. Do not open a market merely to tax their wagons empty.”

Fu Rong reduced the figures with his brush, but warned that spies scouting military positions might pass among the river traders. Fu Jian said goods and permits could be inspected, but the gates must not be closed so tightly that even letters home could not cross. The two argued for half an hour over how far patrols should range along the banks. In the end they sent the Central Army Office to survey the place itself rather than decide by the picture on the palace desk.

The third matter was refugees. Some fled north from Jin territory; others wished to take their families south across the Huai. An official began by asking how they should be entered into the household registers, but Fu Jian asked instead for the placement records of those who had already reached Qin territory. Several widows had been assigned to serve in the households of frontier officers. The county magistrate said they had been settled according to old precedent.
“Find me that precedent,” Fu Jian said.
The magistrate prostrated himself and replied that the practice went back to the years of disorder; a written record might no longer exist.

“An old precedent no one can produce is no grounds for making people sign away their freedom.” Fu Jian pushed the register back. “Have the district first find out who wishes to farm and who has relatives able to take them in. Report the actual numbers in three months.”

Murong Chui had listened to these small disputes without speaking. At last Fu Jian asked whether the garrisons of Hebei could spare some grain for the Huai frontier that winter. Murong answered that they could not easily do so: the garrison fields in Youzhou and Bingzhou had yielded poorly, and there was little fodder for next year’s horses. Draw the stores down too far, and former troops of Yan in Hebei would seize the chance to stir up trouble.
“So even the Champion General has occasions when he refuses to give,” Fu Jian said.

Murong Chui lowered his head, his voice as steady as ever. “When I served in Yan, I saw officers hold up ledgers of empty granaries and call the treasury full. Such words are pleasant to hear. In the end, men’s lives must fill the gap.”

Fu Jian did not rebuke him. He had the warning entered in the record. In that instant he saw that the winter snows of Murong’s northern homeland still lived in his eyes. The man had never forgotten his lost kingdom; nevertheless, he was now willing to argue with the emperor over a shortage of grain for the Qin soldiers standing before them.

At year’s end, Fu Jian restored Fu Hong’s authority to conduct the daily affairs of the Department of State Affairs. The decree was announced at a modest morning audience. The crown prince stood below the steps, still carrying beneath his arm the memorandum on military supply audits he had copied while confined to his residence in the Eastern Palace.
Fu Jian called him forward to place the memorandum upon the imperial desk.
“I struck you that day.”
Heads lifted throughout the hall. Fu Hong held the scroll in his hands. The old mark on the back of one hand had disappeared, but at the words his eyelid moved slightly.
“Your son remembers.”
“Will you dare refuse a seal again?”
“If the numbers in the register do not agree, your son will not dare stamp it.”
“And if I lose my temper again?”
Fu Hong was silent a moment. “Your son will first ask Father to look at it once more.”

Fu Jian did not smile. He placed the decree restoring the crown prince’s authority at the edge of the desk and invited him to inspect the seal impression himself. Fu Hong examined the paper, date, and signatures, took the seal, and certified it. When he returned to his place among the officials, neither father nor son mentioned the slap again.

Discussion turned once more to the limits of military orders. For three years Qin would hold its present defensive lines. If attacked, frontier forces could respond, but pursuit must not be used as a pretext for launching a major campaign to the south. Movements of troops across provincial lines would continue to require verification by three seals. Emergency action in battle could be verified afterward according to existing rules, provided the reasons were recorded. From Luoyang, Fu Pi sent a letter of objection, arguing that with the Jin court so weak, a three-year agreement would squander an opportunity for war. Fu Jian did not suppress it. He ordered the original filed and replied simply: We shall discuss it when you return to the capital.

Zhu Xu stood to one side of the hall, betraying nothing as he heard the decisions on three years of border markets and prisoner exchanges. Fu Jian asked, “Governor Zhu, do you think that after three years our armies might no longer face one another?”
“I cannot answer for the Jin court.”
“Then answer for yourself.”
Zhu Xu thought for a moment. “If the people of Jin are besieged in Xiangyang again, I will defend them again.”
Fu Jian nodded and told the officials to ask no more.

That evening a court historian sought instructions on filing the Fei River dispatches. Could he remove the passages on near-mutiny in the camps, deaths from illness, and unpaid relief? Fu Jian turned to the final page. Damp had spotted the paper, and ink blots half concealed several names. He took up a vermilion brush, circled each obscured name, and ordered it checked and restored rather than erased.

Across the river and far to the south in Jiankang, Xie An was also reading the reports of the withdrawal. Xie Xuan had returned from the front, the river wind still seeming to cling to his clothes. He first recounted the order in which the Qin camps had pulled back, then the places where overzealous Jin pursuit had nearly cost them their boats. Xie An pressed one finger against a small river on the map. “How long did the cavalry the Qin king left behind remain?”
“Until the last grain wagon crossed the muddy slope.”
“Was Murong Chui there?”
“He was.”
Xie An slowly rolled up the map. After a long while he said, “Then we cannot call this their defeat.”

Ministers at the Jin court were already urging a northern campaign to recover Xiangyang. Xie Xuan, however, wanted first to repair the boats, replenish the empty granaries along the Huai, and set the Beifu warships in order. Xie An made no grand display of his nephew’s prudence as the wisdom of a victorious general. He simply told him to repair the leaks already discovered in the bottoms of the boats. The road ahead for Jin would still have to be traveled, stretch by stretch.

That night the watch drums were sounding again inside the palace at Chang’an. Fu Jian had the military map he had brought before Wang Meng’s tomb recopied cleanly and placed among the old papers bound for the historical archive. A pine needle lay caught at the edge of the original map, fallen there at some unknown moment. Fu Jian reached to remove it. The needle broke in two. He studied it for a moment, then shut the document box.

The same moon shone beyond the palace window over the northern lands. A thousand li away, Xie Xuan’s boats lay at anchor across the Fei. Merchants waited for permits to open new crossings. Fu Jian knew there were many decrees still to write. Few of them, perhaps none, would ever be celebrated in a victory song.
